summary.text: For $p=2m+1\equiv3\pmod4$, a quadratic-character sum identity makes $M(m!)M(-m!)^{T}$ skew-symmetric; since $m$ is odd its determinant vanishes, while a polynomial/Vandermonde moment argument shows $M(-m!)$ is nonsingular, forcing $M(m!)$ to be singular. The same argument gives the general criterion that $M(c)$ is nonsingular when $c^m m!\ne1$ modulo $p$, and Wilson’s half-factorial congruence verifies this criterion for $c=m!$ when $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and for $c=-m!$ in the preceding case.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 2\), let \(p=p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime, and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad w=m!.
\]
Since \(n\ge2\), we have \(p\ge3\), so \(p\) is odd and \(p=2m+1\). Let \(\chi:\mathbb F_p\to\{0,\pm1\}\) denote the quadratic character, extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). For an integer \(C\), define the \(m\times m\) integer matrix
\[
L_C=(\chi(i^2-Cj))_{1\le i,j\le m},
\]
where the arguments of \(\chi\) are understood modulo \(p\). Because \(p\) is prime, this is precisely the matrix whose entries are the Legendre (equivalently, Jacobi) symbols in the definition of A226163. Thus
\[
a(n)=\det L_w.
\]
We prove that \(\det L_w=0\) exactly when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\).

We first record several elementary facts that will be used throughout.

1. The residues \(1,2,\ldots,m,-1,-2,\ldots,-m\) are all nonzero and pairwise distinct modulo \(p\), and hence constitute all of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\). Indeed, all the positive representatives involved lie between \(1\) and \(p-1=2m\), and an equality \(r\equiv-s\pmod p\), with \(1\le r,s\le m\), would imply that the positive integer \(r+s<p\) is divisible by \(p\), which is impossible.

2. The squares
\[
r_i=i^2\in\mathbb F_p,\qquad 1\le i\le m,
\]
are pairwise distinct. For if \(i^2=k^2\), then \((i-k)(i+k)=0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). The second factor cannot vanish because \(2\le i+k\le2m=p-1\), so \(i=k\). Moreover, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
r_i^m=i^{2m}=i^{p-1}=1.
\]

3. Wilson's theorem gives the half-factorial identity
\[
w^2=(-1)^{m+1}\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
Indeed,
\[
(p-1)!=\prod_{r=1}^m r(p-r)\equiv(-1)^m(m!)^2=(-1)^m w^2\pmod p,
\]
whereas Wilson's theorem says \((p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p\). Rearranging yields the displayed formula. Notice also that \(w\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), since every factor of \(m!\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(p\).

We next prove the principal nonsingularity lemma.

**Power-matrix lemma.** Let \(c\in\mathbb F_p^\times\). Form the \(m\times m\) matrix
\[
P_c=\bigl((i^2-cj)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}

over \(\mathbb F_p\). If
\[
c^m m!\ne1\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p,
\]
then \(P_c\) is nonsingular.

To prove this, suppose that a vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\in\mathbb F_p^m\) satisfies \(P_cv=0\). For every nonnegative integer \(a\), define its moment
\[
s_a=\sum_{j=1}^m j^a v_j.
\]
For each \(i\), the equation in the \(i\)-th row of \(P_cv=0\), expanded by the binomial theorem, is
\[
0=\sum_{j=1}^m(i^2-cj)^m v_j
 =\sum_{k=0}^m \binom{m}{k}(-c)^{m-k}s_{m-k}(i^2)^k.
\]
Set
\[
q_k=\binom{m}{k}(-c)^{m-k}s_{m-k}\qquad(0\le k\le m).
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m q_k r_i^k=0
\qquad(1\le i\le m),
\]
where \(r_i=i^2\). Since \(r_i^m=1\), this becomes
\[
(q_0+q_m)+q_1r_i+\cdots+q_{m-1}r_i^{m-1}=0
\qquad(1\le i\le m).
\]
The polynomial on the left has degree at most \(m-1\) and vanishes at the \(m\) distinct elements \(r_1,\ldots,r_m\). It must therefore be the zero polynomial. Consequently,
\[
q_0+q_m=0,\qquad q_k=0\quad(1\le k<m).
\]
Now \(q_m=s_0\) and \(q_0=(-c)^m s_m\), so the first of these equations says
\[
(-c)^m s_m+s_0=0. \tag{1}
\]
For \(1\le a<m\), take \(k=m-a\). Then
\[
q_{m-a}=\binom{m}{m-a}(-c)^a s_a=0.
\]
Neither of the first two factors is zero in \(\mathbb F_p\). The power \((-c)^a\) is nonzero because \(c\ne0\). Also \(p\nmid\binom m{m-a}\): the binomial coefficient divides \(m!\), while \(p\nmid m!\). Hence
\[
s_a=0\qquad(1\le a<m). \tag{2}
\]

There is one further relation between \(s_0\) and \(s_m\). Consider
\[
W(X)=\prod_{j=1}^m(X-j)\in\mathbb F_p[X].
\]
Write \(W(X)=\sum_{d=0}^m b_dX^d\). Since \(W(j)=0\) for every \(1\le j\le m\),
\[
0=\sum_{j=1}^m W(j)v_j
 =\sum_{d=0}^m b_d\sum_{j=1}^m j^d v_j
 =\sum_{d=0}^m b_ds_d.
\]
By (2), all the terms with \(1\le d<m\) vanish. The leading coefficient of \(W\) is \(b_m=1\), and its constant coefficient is
\[
b_0=(-1)^m 1\cdot2\cdots m=(-1)^m m!.
\]
Therefore
\[
(-1)^m m!\,s_0+s_m=0. \tag{3}
\]
Substituting \(s_m=-(-1)^m m!s_0\) from (3) into (1), and using
\[
(-c)^m(-1)^m=c^m,
\]
gives
\[
(1-c^m m!)s_0=0.
\]
The hypothesis \(c^m m!\ne1\) implies \(s_0=0\), and then (1) implies \(s_m=0\). Together with (2), this yields
\[
s_a=0\qquad(0\le a<m).
\]
In other words,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m j^a v_j=0\qquad(0\le a<m).
\]
The coefficient matrix of these equations is the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct residues \(1,2,\ldots,m\). Its determinant is
\[
\prod_{1\le r<s\le m}(s-r),
\]
which is nonzero modulo \(p\), since every difference lies strictly between \(0\) and \(p\). Thus \(v=0\). The kernel of \(P_c\) is trivial, proving the power-matrix lemma.

We now connect this lemma to the Legendre-symbol matrices. Euler's criterion, including the case of a zero argument, states that for every \(z\in\mathbb F_p\),
\[
\chi(z)=z^{(p-1)/2}=z^m.
\]
Therefore reduction modulo \(p\) sends \(L_C\) to the matrix
\[
P_{\bar C}=\bigl((i^2-\bar Cj)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},
\]
where \(\bar C\) denotes the residue class of \(C\). Determinants commute with reduction modulo \(p\), so the power-matrix lemma has the following consequence:

If \(\bar C\ne0\) and
\[
\bar C^m m!\ne1\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p,
\]
then \(\det L_C\ne0\) as an integer. Indeed, its reduction modulo \(p\) is the nonzero determinant of \(P_{\bar C}\).

We next establish the character-sum identity needed for the case \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). First, for any nonzero \(d\in\mathbb F_p\),
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x^2-d)=-1. \tag{4}
\]
To see this, count pairs \((x,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2\) satisfying \(y^2=x^2-d\). For each \(x\), the number of possible \(y\)'s is \(1+\chi(x^2-d)\), so the number of pairs is
\[
p+\sum_x\chi(x^2-d).
\]
On the other hand, the equation is \((x-y)(x+y)=d\). Because \(p\) is odd, the change of variables \(u=x-y\), \(v=x+y\) is invertible. The equation \(uv=d\) has exactly \(p-1\) solutions, one for each \(u\ne0\). Equating the two counts proves (4).

It follows that if \(a\ne b\), then
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi((x-a)(x-b))=-1. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(x-a)(x-b)=\frac{(2x-a-b)^2-(a-b)^2}{4}.
\]
The substitution \(z=2x-a-b\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb F_p\), the quantity \((a-b)^2\) is nonzero, and \(1/4\) is a nonzero square, so (5) follows from (4).

Consequently, whenever \(A+B\ne0\),
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi((A-x)(B+x))=-\chi(-1). \tag{6}
\]
For \((A-x)(B+x)=-(x-A)(x-(-B))\), and the two roots \(A\) and \(-B\) are distinct precisely when \(A+B\ne0\); multiplicativity of \(\chi\), followed by (5), gives (6). More generally, if \(c\ne0\), multiplication by \(c\) permutes \(\mathbb F_p\), and hence
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi((A-cx)(B+cx))=-\chi(-1) \tag{7}
\]
under the same condition \(A+B\ne0\).

Assume now that \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(-1\) is not a square modulo \(p\), so
\[
\chi(-1)=-1. \tag{8}
\]
Also, for any nonzero \(a,b\in\mathbb F_p\),
\[
a^2+b^2\ne0. \tag{9}
\]
Otherwise \((a/b)^2=-1\), contradicting the fact that \(-1\) is a nonsquare.

Let \(C\) be any integer whose residue \(c\) is nonzero. Consider the integer matrix
\[
K=L_C L_{-C}^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Its \((i,k)\)-entry is
\[
K_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((i^2-cj)(k^2+cj)\bigr). \tag{10}
\]
We claim that \(K\) is skew-symmetric. To compare \(K_{ik}\) and \(K_{ki}\), rewrite the latter by replacing the positive residues \(j\) with the negative residues \(-j\):
\[
K_{ki}=\sum_{j=1}^m
 \chi\bigl((i^2-c(-j))(k^2+c(-j))\bigr),
\]
after merely commuting the two factors inside \(\chi\). Thus, because the nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_p\) are exactly \(\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm m\}\),
\[
K_{ik}+K_{ki}
 =\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^\times}
   \chi\bigl((i^2-cx)(k^2+cx)\bigr). \tag{11}
\]
By (9), \(i^2+k^2\ne0\). Hence (7), with \(A=i^2\) and \(B=k^2\), applies. In view of (8), the corresponding sum over all of \(\mathbb F_p\) equals
\[
-\chi(-1)=1.
\]
The omitted term at \(x=0\) is
\[
\chi(i^2k^2)=1,
\]
since \(ik\ne0\). Therefore the sum over \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) in (11) is \(1-1=0\). This proves \(K_{ik}+K_{ki}=0\) for every \(i,k\), so
\[
K^{\mathsf T}=-K.
\]

Because \(p=2m+1\equiv3\pmod4\), \(m\) is odd. An odd-order skew-symmetric integer matrix has determinant zero: indeed,
\[
\det K=\det K^{\mathsf T}=\det(-K)=(-1)^m\det K=-\det K,
\]
and hence \(2\det K=0\), which over the integers implies \(\det K=0\). By multiplicativity of determinants and invariance under transpose,
\[
0=\det K=\det L_C\,\det L_{-C}. \tag{12}
\]
Thus, for every nonzero \(C\pmod p\), at least one of the two determinants \(\det L_C\) and \(\det L_{-C}\) vanishes.

We now apply these results with \(C=w=m!\), treating the two possible residue classes of the odd prime \(p\) modulo \(4\).

First suppose
\[
p\equiv1\pmod4.
\]
Then \(m\) is even and \(m+1\) is odd. The half-factorial identity gives
\[
w^2=(-1)^{m+1}=-1. \tag{13}
\]
We claim that
\[
w^m w=w^{m+1}\ne1. \tag{14}
\]
If instead \(w^{m+1}=1\), then squaring and using (13) would give
\[
1=(w^{m+1})^2=(w^2)^{m+1}=(-1)^{m+1}=-1,
\]
which is impossible in \(\mathbb F_p\) because \(p\ne2\). Thus (14) holds. The power-matrix lemma and the reduction by Euler's criterion, applied with \(c=w\), show that
\[
\det L_w\ne0.
\]
Therefore \(a(n)\ne0\) whenever \(p_n\equiv1\pmod4\).

Now suppose
\[
p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Then \(m\) is odd, so \(m+1\) is even. The half-factorial identity now gives
\[
w^2=(-1)^{m+1}=1.
\]
It follows that
\[
w^{m+1}=1,
\]
because \(m+1\) is even. Hence
\[
(-w)^m w=(-1)^m w^{m+1}=-1. \tag{15}
\]
In particular, \((-w)^m w\ne1\), again because \(p\ne2\). Applying the power-matrix lemma and Euler-criterion reduction with \(c=-w\) proves
\[
\det L_{-w}\ne0. \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, (12), applied with \(C=w\), says
\[
\det L_w\,\det L_{-w}=0.
\]
Together with (16), this forces
\[
\det L_w=0.
\]
Thus \(a(n)=0\) whenever \(p_n\equiv3\pmod4\).

Finally, every odd prime is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\) modulo \(4\). Since \(n\ge2\) ensures that \(p_n\) is odd, the two cases above exhaust all possibilities. We have therefore proved
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }
\]
for every \(n\ge2\), as claimed.
